tier_reason: The current README states only the authors' '1.5x to 7x as fast as pyahocorasick' range; benchmarks/test_comparison.py is public, but no compiler, flags, Python or pyahocorasick version, or CPU is given. The older PyPI 0.14.0 README (2023-04-25) has per-case ops/s numbers, also first-party and without hardware. That is first-party evidence with partial methodology, so tier C.

corrections.claimed_speedup: Current README: 'I've seen ahocorasick_rs run 1.5x to 7x as fast as pyahocorasick, depending on the options used' (no per-case numbers). The older README on PyPI 0.14.0 (2023-04-25) has ops/s, higher is better. Long case (~4,000 patterns, ~700-char lines): longest match 436,000 vs 65,000 (about 6.7x, derived from page data); overlapping 329,000 vs 76,000 (about 4.3x, derived). Short case (~10 patterns, ~70-char lines): longest 1,930,000 vs 1,120,000 (about 1.7x, derived); overlapping 1,250,000 vs 880,000 (about 1.4x, derived).
corrections.workload: pytest-benchmark in benchmarks/test_comparison.py. Long case: about 4,200 first-name patterns (names longer than 4 characters) searched in 100,000 haystacks of roughly 600 characters. Short case: 10 patterns over 10,000 short haystacks. Like-for-like pairs are pyahocorasick iter (overlapping) vs find_matches_as_strings(overlapping=True), and iter_long vs MatchKind.LeftmostLongest; the default Standard (non-overlapping) runs have no pyahocorasick counterpart. The file's comment says 90% of long haystacks have no match and 10% have one, but the generator inserts a name into only every 90th haystack (about 1.1%).
corrections.caveats: The current README gives only a 1.5x to 7x range with no per-case numbers, hardware or versions. The per-case table (436k vs 65k ops/s and so on) appears only in the older 0.14.0 README from 2023 and was measured on an unstated machine. Both sides are measured through Python, so call and string-conversion overhead is included (pyo3 UTF-8 conversion on the Rust side; the benchmark varies haystacks on purpose so this overhead is not hidden). The comparison is not language-level. ahocorasick_rs is a pyo3 binding of BurntSushi's Rust aho-corasick crate, which adds SIMD prefilters (including the packed Teddy searcher for small pattern sets) and DFA or contiguous-NFA layouts that pyahocorasick's trie lacks, so the short-pattern wins are probably prefilter wins rather than codegen. pyahocorasick's setup.py sets no optimisation flags (it inherits CPython's sysconfig CFLAGS), so the C baseline's opt level is unknown. The benchmark code's own comment on the match fraction contradicts its generator (about 1.1% of long haystacks have a match, not 10%).
corrections.why_faster: Both sides are Aho-Corasick in name only. The Rust aho-corasick crate wrapped by ahocorasick_rs uses vectorized prefilters (memchr-based and the packed Teddy SIMD searcher for small pattern sets, per the crate's lib.rs docs) and offers DFA and contiguous-NFA automata. pyahocorasick walks a pointer-based trie with fail links. Matching on str also releases the GIL, which does not matter in this single-threaded benchmark.

notes: Real claim backed by a public pytest-benchmark file, but the current README carries only an anecdotal 1.5x-7x range; the concrete ops/s table exists only in the 2023 0.14.0 README on PyPI. The speed belongs to BurntSushi's Rust aho-corasick crate (not listed in the catalog); this entry is its Python binding, and the orchestrator may prefer to file the crate itself. tier_reason: The README tables are copied verbatim from benchmarks/benchmark-results.md, which scripts/benchmark-vs-awk.sh generates. Code and CPU (Apple M5 Max) are public. The rustc version is not stated, and gawk/mawk are Homebrew bottles (/opt/homebrew/bin) with unknown build flags. First-party, missing compiler and baseline flags, so tier C.

corrections.claimed_speedup: README tables (hyperfine mean ms on 1M-line inputs, Apple M5 Max). Rows are awkrs (JIT) / awkrs (bytecode) vs mawk 1.3.4 vs gawk 5.4.0. { print $1 }: 15.7 / 16.1 vs 66.2 vs 100.8 (mawk relative 4.22x). Sum first column: 13.0 / 12.9 vs 37.5 vs 62.9 (2.90x). Multi-field print: 56.4 / 55.8 vs 156.6 vs 266.1 (2.81x). Regex filter: 11.1 / 11.1 vs 19.3 vs 351.4 (mawk 1.74x, gawk 31.72x). Associative array: 340.0 / 343.7 vs 610.0 vs 342.4 (parity with gawk). NR%2 field print: 30.2 / 30.7 vs 71.1 vs 116.1 (2.36x). Field computation: 19.0 / 18.8 vs 57.7 vs 100.5 (3.08x). String concat print: 51.0 / 50.5 vs 121.0 vs 182.2 (2.39x). No-match gsub: 13.8 / 13.9 vs 74.3 vs 436.3 (mawk 5.39x). CPU-bound BEGIN loop: 9.2 / 9.6 vs 9.7 vs 20.7 (mawk 1.06x, within noise). Generated 2026-04-10 with awkrs 0.1.18. The README says the bytecode row represents today's default path for these programs.
corrections.compiler_and_flags: awkrs: cargo build --release with the default release profile (no [profile.release] in Cargo.toml, so opt-level 3, no LTO); rustc version not stated. Baselines: Homebrew bottles /opt/homebrew/bin/gawk (GNU Awk 5.4.0) and /opt/homebrew/bin/mawk (1.3.4 20260302), build flags not stated. BSD awk is /usr/bin/awk. Locale is not pinned (the script does not set LC_ALL).
corrections.caveats: First-party, single machine (Apple M5 Max, macOS 25.4). Numbers are from awkrs 0.1.18 (2026-04-10) while the crate is now 0.5.7, so they have not been re-run on current code. The README's 2026-06-01 caveat says the JIT rows came from a Cranelift module that has since been removed; the bytecode rows are within 0.5 ms. The wins come from special-cased fast paths, not from Rust codegen: single-rule programs such as { print $1 }, { s += $1 } and no-match literal gsub are recognised and run as raw byte scans over an mmap'd file, skipping the VM. The baselines run their general record loops through read(). Baseline flags are unknown (Homebrew bottles, probably distro-default -O2, not a verified -O3). The locale is not set, and gawk's 351 ms regex and 436 ms gsub rows may reflect UTF-8 multibyte matching, while awkrs works on bytes. Each hyperfine time includes process startup on 10-25 ms runs. Parity only on the associative-array case (gawk) and the BEGIN loop (mawk). The repo has 1 star and no third-party reproduction.
corrections.why_faster: Workload-specific fast paths rather than language codegen. Regular files are memory-mapped. print $N and s += $N with the default FS scan raw bytes for the Nth field and skip the VM. A no-match literal gsub becomes a memmem scan that writes lines straight from the mapped buffer. Everything else runs on a peephole-fused superinstruction bytecode VM with zero-copy field ranges, a direct 64 KB output buffer and cached separators. The fusevm/Cranelift offload does not engage on these string/field programs. Default -j 1, so no parallelism in the tables.

notes: Numbers match the README and benchmarks/benchmark-results.md exactly; the record omitted the gsub row (now added). Keep at C with these shortcomings: stale (measured on 0.1.18), wins from mmap/raw-byte special-case paths rather than the language, Homebrew baseline flags unknown, locale unpinned (gawk regex/gsub rows suspect), 1 star. tier_reason: The README's criterion tables compare against simdutf (C++) via the simdutf crate, and the bench code (benches/codec.rs) is public. The rustc and C++ compiler versions are not stated and the x86 CPU is only 'AMD EPYC, Zen 2' in a 4-vCPU VM with no model. First-party, missing compiler and exact CPU, so tier C.

corrections.claimed_speedup: README criterion throughput, encodify vs simdutf (C++ via the simdutf 0.7 crate), 64 KiB. Apple M5 Max (NEON): Base64 encode 25.73 vs 25.95 GB/s (1.0x, simdutf marginally ahead); decode 18.12 vs 15.38 (1.2x); MIME encode with CRLF 21.27 vs simdutf LF-only 14.35 (1.5x); MIME decode 14.08 vs 10.08 (1.4x). AMD EPYC Zen 2 (AVX2, 4-vCPU VM): encode 19.17 vs 13.96 (1.4x); decode 14.97 vs 11.23 (1.3x); MIME encode 10.72 vs 9.50 (1.1x); MIME decode 8.61 vs 5.20 (1.7x). At 32 B: simdutf decode is about 3x slower (Apple 2.02 vs 6.08, AMD 0.56 vs 1.63); simdutf leads Apple MIME encode (5.75 vs 4.50) and AMD plain encode (1.99 vs 1.88). Against the fastest crate overall, the summary table shows parity with Rust base64-turbo for plain Base64 on AMD (19.2 and 15.0 GB/s, 1.0x).
corrections.compiler_and_flags: Criterion via 'cargo bench --bench codec' (bench profile inherits release opt-level 3, debug = true); benchmarks need Rust 1.93 or later, exact rustc not stated. simdutf C++ (version 7.7.1, vendored by simdutf-rs 0.7.0) is compiled by the cc crate with -std=c++17 and no explicit optimisation flags, so it takes cargo's opt-level (-O3 under the bench profile, inferred from cc defaults). C++ compiler not stated.
corrections.caveats: New first-party repo: 3 commits, 1.0.0 published 2026-09-28, 1.0.2 on 2026-10-02. The C++ baseline is simdutf 7.7.1 as vendored by the simdutf-rs 0.7.0 crate (February 2026), not necessarily current upstream. It is called through a Rust FFI wrapper that cannot be inlined, which inflates its per-call overhead at 32 B and 1 KiB. The simdutf MIME-encode rows emit LF only (fewer bytes than encodify's CRLF), which if anything favours simdutf. Plain Base64 against simdutf is parity only for Apple encode; elsewhere encodify leads simdutf by 1.2x to 1.4x. The fastest rival there is the Rust base64-turbo crate at parity. The x86 machine is a 4-vCPU Zen 2 VM with no model given. Not a language-level claim: the win comes from hand-written NEON/SSSE3/AVX2 kernels and a fused CRLF line-wrapping path versus simdutf's own SIMD kernels. No third-party reproduction.
corrections.stars_or_usage: 1 star, 0 forks, 3 commits; crates.io 858 downloads (encodify 1.0.2; first published 2026-09-28)
corrections.why_faster: Different hand-written SIMD kernels (NEON on aarch64, SSSE3/AVX2 with runtime detection on x86), with MIME 76-column CRLF wrapping and line-aware decoding fused into the kernels, and output written into caller-owned slices without zero-filling. simdutf is reached through an FFI call that cannot be inlined, which accounts for much of its small-input deficit.

notes: Numbers match the README; the record's 'plain Base64 is parity with simdutf' holds only for Apple encode (AMD shows 1.3x-1.4x over simdutf; the 1.0x there is against Rust base64-turbo). simdutf is already listed (wave 7, https://github.com/simdutf/simdutf), so baseline_in_list is true. Shortcomings to record: brand-new 3-commit repo, first-party only, simdutf 7.7.1 via an FFI wrapper (small-size rows penalised), C++ build flags inferred from cc defaults, EPYC model not given.
